query_text: how do you type up minutes of a meeting

parts.text:
Typing up meeting minutes is a crucial skill that ensures everyone is on the same page regarding decisions made, tasks assigned, and next steps. Meeting minutes are not a verbatim transcript of everything said; instead, they are a clear, objective summary of the meeting's outcomes.

Here is a step-by-step guide on how to prepare, write, and format professional meeting minutes, along with a standard template you can use.

---

### Phase 1: Preparation (Before the Meeting)
A little preparation makes typing up the minutes much easier afterward.
*   **Get the Agenda:** Ask the meeting organizer for the agenda beforehand. This will serve as your outline.
*   **Create a Template:** Set up your document with placeholders for the date, time, attendees, and agenda items (see the template below).
*   **Know Your Role:** If you are the minute-taker, focus on taking notes rather than actively participating in the debate. 

---

### Phase 2: Taking Notes (During the Meeting)
Don't try to write down every single sentence. Focus on capturing the most important information:
*   **Decisions:** What was agreed upon? (e.g., "The budget was approved.")
*   **Action Items:** Who is doing what, and by when? (e.g., "Sarah to send the updated design by Friday, Nov 10.")
*   **Main Discussion Points:** Briefly summarize the arguments for and against a decision, without naming every single speaker unless necessary.
*   **Key Information:** Record the date, start/end times, and list of attendees (including those who sent apologies for being absent).

---

### Phase 3: Writing and Formatting (After the Meeting)
Try to type up the minutes **within 24 hours** while the conversation is still fresh in your mind. 

*   **Keep it Objective:** Write in a neutral, third-person tone (e.g., "The marketing team proposed..." instead of "We thought that..."). Avoid recording personal opinions or emotional language.
*   **Use Clear Headings:** Group notes by agenda items so they are easy to navigate.
*   **Use Bullet Points:** Blocks of text are hard to read. Use bullet points for discussions and bold text for action items.
*   **Be Concise:** If a discussion lasted 20 minutes but resulted in no decisions, summarize it in one or two sentences.
*   **Proofread:** Check for spelling, grammatical errors, and clarity. 

---

### A Standard Meeting Minutes Template

Use this format to structure your document:

```text
[COMPANY/ORGANIZATION NAME]
MEETING MINUTES

Meeting Name: [e.g., Q3 Marketing Strategy Review]
Date: [e.g., October 24, 2026]
Time: [e.g., 10:00 AM – 11:00 AM EST]
Location: [e.g., Conference Room B / Zoom]

1. ATTENDEES
• Present: [Name, Title], [Name, Title], [Name, Title]
• Apologies (Absent): [Name, Title]
• Minute Taker: [Your Name]

2. APPROVAL OF PREVIOUS MINUTES
• The minutes of the previous meeting held on [Date] were approved [with/without] corrections.

3. AGENDA ITEMS & DISCUSSION

Topic 1: [Name of Agenda Item]
• Discussion: Summary of key points discussed. (e.g., "The team reviewed the current social media metrics. Engagement is up 15%, but conversion rates remain flat.")
• Decision: [e.g., "It was decided to pivot the ad budget toward LinkedIn rather than Instagram."]
• Action Item: [Name] to [Task] by [Deadline].

Topic 2: [Name of Agenda Item]
• Discussion: Summary...
• Decision: ...
• Action Item: [Name] to [Task] by [Deadline].

4. ACTION ITEM SUMMARY (Quick reference list)
• [Name] – [Task to complete] – Due by [Date]
• [Name] – [Task to complete] – Due by [Date]

5. NEXT MEETING
• Date: [Date of next meeting]
• Time: [Time]
• Location: [Location/Link]

Minutes submitted by: [Your Name]
```

---

### 3 Golden Rules for Minute-Takers
1.  **Clarify if you are unsure:** If a decision is made or a task is assigned and you didn't catch who is responsible or what the deadline is, interrupt politely and ask: *"Just to make sure I capture this correctly in the minutes, who is taking ownership of this action item?"*
2.  **Stick to facts, not drama:** If a heated argument breaks out, do not record the emotional exchange. Simply write: *"The team discussed concerns regarding the timeline."*
3.  **Get approval before sending:** Once written, send the draft to the chairperson or meeting organizer for a quick review before distributing it to the entire team.
